name: Golden ratio maxx

card.summary: A facial-analysis approach that compares a person's facial measurements with 1.618 proportions to decide which features to improve for a more harmonious look.
card.note: Researchers report that attractiveness is not tied to a single ratio.

quick.overview:
Golden ratio maxx is a looksmaxxing method in which someone measures their face, often on a photo or a morph, against the golden ratio of about 1.618 and uses the gaps to decide what to change. Proportions commonly checked include face length to width and the spacing of the eyes, nose and mouth.

The appeal is a concrete target: the result can point to a haircut, grooming, makeup, or in some cases surgery. Research on facial attractiveness points more to averageness, symmetry and other cues than to one ratio.
quick.how: Users overlay grids or masks on front-facing photos, compare their numbers with ideal ratios, and sometimes morph their photo to preview changes. On looksmax.org one poster described planning to morph a photo and then look up the surgeries needed.
quick.risks: The method is a measuring exercise with no direct physical risk. Concerns arise when the measurements drive surgical decisions, since replies in the thread questioned whether a teenager should be thinking about surgery while the jaws are still growing.

lead: Golden ratio maxx is a looksmaxxing method that applies the golden ratio, about 1.618, to facial measurements. Practitioners compare ratios in their own face to this figure and treat the differences as a list of things to adjust [1].

Interest in the idea reaches back to claims that human proportions follow divine proportion; Kepler said the image of man and woman stems from it, and Le Corbusier built a body-scale system on it [2]. Wikipedia notes that the idea that the ratio underlies human beauty is popular but often unsupported [2].

Facial attractiveness research has highlighted averageness and symmetry, and a 2008 Italian study found attractive adolescents tended to have larger forehead-to-face ratios and smaller nasal volume [3].

chain: Face closer to the target proportions
angle.text: Followers use the ratios as a map for deciding what to change, such as hairstyle, facial hair or procedures. Whether closer ratios raise attractiveness is a matter researchers have not settled.

paras: The method treats the golden ratio as a template for harmony. Users take front-facing photos and measure proportions between facial landmarks, then compare each with the target [1].

A looksmax.org thread titled Golden Ratio maxx has a poster saying they plan to try the method, morph a photo, and look up needed surgeries. Another user asked why a 14-year-old was thinking of surgery, and the poster replied they were not and that jaw growth continues from 16 to 20 [1].

Wikipedia's golden ratio article reports that a 1999 study of 565 paintings found artists generally did not use golden-ratio canvas proportions and that claims about the ratio in the body are often unsupported [2]. Attractiveness research instead discusses averageness, where averaged faces were rated more attractive, and symmetry [3].

lore.intro: The method appears in looksmax.org threads as a way to plan changes [1].

claims.claim: Matching 1.618 proportions makes a face more attractive
claims.believers: Proponents use the ratio as a goal for grooming and procedures and plan changes from morphs [1].
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes the idea that the ratio underlies human beauty as popular but often unsupported, and attractiveness research highlights averageness and symmetry [2][3].
